facts.text: A Performance Level (PL) is a five-step grade, written a to e, specifying how reliably a machine safety function must work; the Category describes the circuit architecture used to reach that grade.
facts.quote: A Performance Level is a five-step grade, written a to e, that says how reliably a safety function on a machine must work, and the Category describes the circuit architecture used to reach that grade.

facts.text: Under ISO 13849-1, PL a is the lowest Performance Level and PL e is the highest.
facts.quote: The Performance Level of ISO 13849-1 does the same for safety functions on machines: PL a is the lowest, PL e the highest.

facts.text: The required Performance Level (PLr) comes from the risk assessment.
facts.quote: The required level (PLr) comes from the risk assessment.

facts.text: The achieved Performance Level depends on Category, mean time to dangerous failure of the parts (MTTFd), diagnostic coverage (DC), and protection against common-cause failure.
facts.quote: The achieved level comes from four things.

facts.text: Performance Level Categories B, 1, 2, 3 and 4 describe architectures ranging from a single well-built channel to two mutually monitoring channels so that one fault cannot remove the safety function.
facts.quote: The Category (B, 1, 2, 3 or 4) is the architecture, from a single well-built channel to two channels that monitor each other so one fault cannot remove the function.

facts.text: Performance Levels correspond to bands of average probability of dangerous failure per hour; PL a allows between one dangerous failure per 10,000 hours and one per 100,000 hours.
facts.quote: Each PL is a band of average probability of a dangerous failure per hour: PL a allows between one in 10,000 hours and one in 100,000

facts.text: The passage describes PL e as demanding fewer than one dangerous failure per 10 million hours and gives its probability band as between 10^-8 and 10^-7 per hour.
facts.quote: PL e demands fewer than one in 10 million hours (between 10^-8 and 10^-7 per hour).

facts.text: ISO 13849-1:2023 is the generic machinery method, including software, but does not itself assign the level required for the collision function; ISO 19014 is the sector framework for earth-moving machines.
facts.quote: ISO 13849-1:2023 is the generic machinery method, including software, but does not itself assign the level this collision function needs; for earth-moving machines the sector framework is ISO 19014 [Chapter 3]

facts.text: ISO 13849-2:2012 lists simulation among its validation methods, including software simulation of faults.
facts.quote: The validation part, ISO 13849-2:2012, lists simulation among its validation methods, including software simulation of faults [Chapter 12].

facts.text: The booklet recommends ISO 13849 or IEC 62061 for the intervention chain in a safety-case skeleton.
facts.quote: The booklet suggests ISO 13849 or IEC 62061 for the intervention chain in a safety-case skeleton [Chapter 1]

facts.text: The booklet expects the internal safety board to work under ISO 19014 and ISO 13849.
facts.quote: expects the internal safety board to work under ISO 19014 and ISO 13849 [Chapter 2].

facts.text: The required Performance Level drives architecture and validation effort as much as threshold tuning does; a higher level means more redundancy, more diagnostics and more evidence.
facts.quote: The required level drives architecture and validation effort as much as threshold tuning does [Chapter 8]; a higher level means more redundancy, more diagnostics and more evidence.
